posts.caption: Somebody laminated a sign for the tack room door last week. Please keep animals out, it said, in three different fonts. By Tuesday morning Big Red had her whole head in there, glasses fogged, looking over the saddle racks like a manager reviewing inventory. I let her stay. The sign was written by a woman who has never tried to move an eighteen-hundred-pound mare who has decided the fly spray is hers. She backed out when she was finished, one careful step at a time. The sign is still up. It's mostly decorative now.
posts.first: My first barn had a rule that nobody rode before eight. Nobody told the horses, and nobody told the roosters. Forty years later I still wake up at five and look out the window like someone owes me an explanation. Nobody has ever come forward.

posts.caption: The evening feed goes in at five, and by five-fifteen the barn is quiet except for chewing. That's when she drags the green bucket over, turns it upside down, and sits in the aisle with her coffee gone cold. She talks to the old gelding about the day, the weather, the price of shavings. He chews and listens. Some nights she forgets what she came to say and just sits there. He doesn't mind. The lights go off at seven. She says it's for the horses. I've watched long enough to know better.
posts.first: My dad did this with his old mare every night until he was seventy-nine. He'd walk out with a flashlight he didn't need and stay an hour. I asked him once what they talked about. He said mostly nothing, and that it was the best conversation he'd had all day.

posts.theme: the horse budget vs. the spouse
posts.quote: Last summer I spent more on fly spray than on groceries. The flies are still doing better than I am.
posts.first: I keep the fly spray receipts in the glove box, the way other people keep evidence. My husband found one in August and asked if we were running a farm. I told him it's a very small farm. He went back inside without another word.

posts.caption: The paddock turned to soup after four days of rain, and the entire barn has stopped pretending to care. Every horse on the property is brown to the elbows. Except one. She picks her way along the fence line on the dry strip like she's crossing a ballroom, lifting each hoof as if the ground might owe her money. Naturally she ended up with a single splash on her left knee. She looked at it for a full minute. Then at me. I've been sentenced to a bucket and a sponge.
posts.first: I bathed this mare on a Thursday in March for a show we didn't win. She stayed clean for forty minutes. I found her in the arena rolling like a puppy and didn't have the heart to stop her. We drove home in silence, and she was thrilled.

posts.caption: First morning below freezing and the whole barn changes. The water trough needs the heater, the blankets come out of the bins smelling like last winter, and the horses stop asking for anything but breakfast. Nobody has a show on the calendar. The trail rides slow to a stroll and then to nothing. I used to dread it. This year I bought a better thermos and a good pair of insulated gloves, and I stopped feeling guilty about the slower days. The mare in stall four seems to have understood this long before I did.
posts.first: My mother used to say winter was the farm's way of making people sit down. She said it knitting in the kitchen with the barn light on out the window. I rolled my eyes for about thirty years. This is the first winter I've said it back to her.

posts.caption: The fence on the north side is four feet high and freshly tightened, and I have personally checked it twice. This morning the small pony was standing in the yard by the mailbox like he was waiting for the mail. I walked the whole line looking for a gap and found nothing. Nothing except one bottom rail that sits about eight inches off the ground, and a flat spot in the mud with a pony-shaped dent. I ordered new boards yesterday. He watched me carry them in and ate a dandelion.
posts.first: The vet once told me Shetlands are the Houdinis of the barn. I laughed. Last spring I found Pudding standing in my vegetable garden holding a head of lettuce, with the gate latched behind him. I've stopped trying to understand it and started buying heavier chains.
